sections.title: Luminaire and lighting outlet
sections.plain_explanation:
A luminaire is the complete lighting unit — lamp or LED source, the parts that distribute the light, position and protect the source, and connect it to the supply. It is the Code's word for what crews call a fixture, and the Code uses luminaire everywhere a rule means the whole unit, not just the bulb.
• Luminaire: the whole unit, source to housing.
• Lighting outlet: an outlet intended to connect directly to a luminaire or a lampholder — the box and circuit point.
• Every lighting outlet is an outlet; not every outlet is a lighting outlet.
sections.on_the_job: Fixture counts on a takeoff are luminaire counts. When a rule or a plan says 'lighting outlet,' it means the box and circuit point, whether or not the luminaire itself has been set yet — rough-in is inspected against outlets, trim against luminaires. On a Marion Oaks new-build takeoff, price the outlets — box, circuit point, switch leg — at rough-in and the luminaires at trim, and the two counts reconcile when the builder's fixtures finally arrive.

sections.why_it_exists: Counts, loads and inspections all key off these two words. If the fixture count and the lighting outlet count drift apart, the takeoff, the circuit load and the rough-in inspection stop agreeing — and the miss surfaces later as a change order or a failed rough-in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'luminaire' means the lamp or the bulb. It means the complete unit. The companion trap treats the lighting outlet as the fixture itself — the outlet is the box and circuit point, and it exists, and gets inspected, before any luminaire is set.

sections.title: Service — the family of service terms
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 splits 'service' into a family of terms, and the rules in Article 230 hang on the differences.
• Service: the conductors and equipment for delivering electric energy from the serving utility to the wiring system of the premises served.
• Service point: the point where the utility's facilities meet the premises wiring — the boundary of responsibility.
• Service conductors: the conductors from the service point to the service disconnecting means. Overhead, they divide into the service drop and the service-entrance conductors; underground, the utility's run is the service lateral.
• Service drop: the overhead conductors from the utility's system to the service point — the utility's side.
• Service-entrance conductors: on the customer's side, from the service point to the service equipment.
• Service equipment: the gear — usually the main disconnect, its overcurrent devices and their enclosure — that controls and cuts off the supply to the building.
sections.on_the_job: Find the service point first on any service change. It decides whose rules govern each run of conductor and where the grounded and grounding conductors are bonded together. On a 200 A upgrade in Ocala, Sharma's NEC work starts at the service point: the meter sits outside and the panel inside, back to back (S-09), with new Siemens service equipment, while the drop and the utility's side follow the serving utility's own requirements.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the house allows. The working-space rules of 110.26 still apply in full to that panel.
sections.figure_idea: One-line from utility pole through drop, meter and main disconnect into the panel, with service point, service conductors and service equipment labelled.
sections.florida_note: The utility serving the job (for example FPL or a municipal utility) sets its own service-point and meter requirements alongside the NEC. Confirm the utility's current requirements on service work.

sections.title: Service conductors, drop, lateral, entrance, equipment, and point
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 splits the service into named pieces, and each name carries an owner. Learn the pieces and most service arguments settle themselves.
• Service point: the point where the utility's facilities meet the premises wiring. It is the boundary of responsibility — the utility's rules govern on its side of the point, the NEC governs on ours.
• Service conductors: the conductors from the service point to the service disconnecting means.
• Service drop: the utility's overhead conductors, from its system to the service point.
• Service-entrance conductors: the customer-side run, from the service point to the service equipment. The overhead and underground definitions name the same job two ways.
• Service lateral: the utility's underground run to the service point.
• Service equipment: the gear — usually the main disconnect and its enclosure — that controls and cuts off the supply to the building.
The base Service page introduces the family; this page is the map of who owns what, where.
sections.on_the_job: Nearly every service argument is a service-point argument: whose conductor, whose repair, whose standard. On Sharma services the meter sits outside and the panel inside, back to back, so the service-entrance run stays as short as the layout allows — and the utility's requirements govern everything on its side of the point. After a storm in Marion County, a limb takes down the overhead drop and bends the mast. The drop is the utility's to restring; the mast and the entrance conductors below the weatherhead are the customer's — Sharma's repair, permitted and inspected.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the layout allows — the arrangement that keeps the service-entrance conductors short.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Underground, the utility's run is the lateral. 'Drop' is overhead only.

sections.title: In sight from — and disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Two linked terms decide where disconnects can go.
• Disconnecting means: the device, or group of devices, that disconnects a circuit's conductors from their supply — a breaker or a disconnect switch are the everyday examples.
• In sight from: equipment is in sight from other equipment when it is visible from it and not more than 50 ft away. Both halves must hold at the same time.
A disconnect 20 ft away but hidden behind a wall is not in sight. A disconnect in plain view at 75 ft is not in sight either. Many equipment articles require the disconnect to be in sight from the equipment it serves — or lockable, where the article allows the out-of-sight route; 110.25 covers lockable disconnecting means.
sections.on_the_job: When you set a condenser or air-handler disconnect, stand at the equipment and look. A typical house condenser: the disconnect is on the wall 15 ft away, in plain view — in sight, done. If the only wall space puts it around the corner of the house, or the run stretches past 50 ft along a long commercial wall, the in-sight option is not met, and the conversation about a lockable disconnect or a relocation happens before trim-out, not at the final.
sections.figure_idea: A condenser with a sight line drawn to its disconnect on the wall 15 ft away marked in sight, and a second disconnect drawn behind a fence marked not in sight.
sections.why_it_exists: The disconnect is what a worker reaches for when a unit starts, smokes or traps someone. If the person at the equipment can see it, nobody can re-energize the circuit from around a corner while hands are inside the unit — and the worker does not have to hunt for it in an emergency. The 50 ft cap keeps the word 'visible' honest: a speck at the far end of a warehouse is not control of the equipment.
inspection_fails: Condenser disconnect mounted around the corner of the house, out of sight of the unit it serves.
Disconnect visible from the equipment but more than 50 ft away.
Disconnect in sight of the wrong unit — two condensers sharing one disconnect with no marking of what it controls.
Disconnect for rooftop equipment located inside the building, out of sight of the equipment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer keeps only half of the definition. 'Visible from the equipment' at 75 ft is not in sight, and '20 ft away' behind a wall is not in sight. Both halves — visible, and not more than 50 ft away — must be true at the same time.

sections.title: Device, disconnecting means, and switch types
sections.plain_explanation:
Three layers of words keep the disconnect rules straight.
• Device: a unit of an electrical system, other than a conductor, that carries or controls electric energy. Switches, receptacles, breakers and thermostats are devices; wire and conduit are not.
• Disconnecting means: a device, a group of devices, or another means by which the conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source. It is the thing the In Sight page measures from — visible, and not more than 50 ft away.
• General-use switch: controls lighting and appliance loads, and is rated in amperes at its marked voltage.
• Isolating switch: meant to isolate a circuit from its source. It has no interrupting rating and is not intended to interrupt current under load.
• Motor-circuit switch: rated in horsepower, and built to interrupt the maximum operating overload current of the motor it serves.
sections.on_the_job: An isolating switch is not a load-break switch — opening one under load is an arc event, not a disconnect. When a rule calls for a disconnecting means, check that the device in hand is actually rated to do the disconnecting job for that load type. On a rooftop change-out, the crew kills the load at the breaker first and only then opens the isolating switch beside the unit; the disconnect that serves the condenser still has to sit in sight of it — visible and within 50 ft.

sections.why_it_exists: A disconnect is a promise: pull it, and the equipment is dead. The promise only holds if the device was built to break the load in front of it. An isolating switch opened under load draws an arc it was never designed to quench, in front of the person holding the handle. The definitions are the warning label — they tell you which switch keeps the promise and which one never made it.
inspection_fails: Isolating switch opened under load — arc damage at the blades; it was never rated to break that current.
Thermostat accepted as the disconnecting means for a rooftop unit — a control device is not a disconnect.
Condenser disconnect out of sight of the unit and past 50 ft — fails the in-sight rule these definitions feed.
General-use snap switch carrying a motor load it was never rated to switch.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats every switch as a disconnect. An isolating switch can serve as a disconnecting means for isolation, but it is not built to interrupt load current — and a thermostat, though it is a device, is a control, not a disconnecting means for the equipment it runs.

sections.title: Premises wiring, separately derived systems, raceway, and splices
sections.plain_explanation:
Five Article 100 words that draw the map of a job:
• Premises wiring system: all the wiring inside a building and attached to it, from the service point — or from another power source such as a generator or a solar system — out to the outlets. It does not include the internal wiring of equipment itself.
• Separately derived system: a premises wiring system fed from a source other than a service — a transformer, generator, converter or battery — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply conductors of another system, other than through grounding and bonding.
• Raceway: an enclosed channel built to hold conductors or cables. Conduit and tubing are raceways; a cable assembly is not.
• Splice: the connection between conductors. A splicing wire connector — a wire nut, lever connector or terminal block — is the device listed to make that connection under pressure.
• Hoistway: the shaft-like space an elevator, dumbwaiter or similar equipment travels in. It has its own wiring rules in Article 620.
sections.on_the_job: A transformer in a small Orlando medical office steps 480 V down to 208Y/120 V for a panel. That panel is a separately derived system, which is why it gets its own neutral-to-ground bond through a system bonding jumper — the bond the Grounding family page describes. And every splice the crew makes on the same job lives or dies by the connector's listing: the connector, not the tape over it, is the splice.

sections.why_it_exists: These words decide where one system ends and another begins — and that decides where the neutral gets bonded, which fill and support rules apply, and whether a connection is legal at all. Call a transformer-fed panel "just another panel" and its bonding jumper gets missed. Call a cable a raceway and every rule you reach for afterward is the wrong one.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "The standby generator makes this a separately derived system." Not by itself. The definition turns on the connection — if the generator's grounded conductor stays solidly connected to the service's, there is a direct electrical connection and the system is not separately derived. It becomes separately derived only when that connection is broken, as with a switched neutral.

sections.title: Special permission
sections.plain_explanation:
Special permission is the written consent of the AHJ, given where the Code says the AHJ may allow an alternative. It is not a verbal okay from a plans examiner, a builder or a homeowner, and it is not something an electrician grants himself. Where the Code requires it, get it in writing before the work is done.
• Written — if it is not on paper, it is not special permission.
• From the AHJ — the authority enforcing the Code on that job (90.4), not the builder, the owner or the supply house.
• Before the work — consent chased after the fact is an argument, not a permission.
• Only where the Code contemplates it — the AHJ grants special permission where the rules allow it; the rest of the rules have no such door.
sections.on_the_job: If a job depends on special permission, paper it: keep the AHJ's written consent with the permit documents so the next inspector sees the same record. A note in the job file saying 'the inspector was fine with it' is not the consent — get the signed approval itself, and file it where the final inspector will find it.
sections.why_it_exists: The written rule protects everybody on the job. The next inspector sees the same record the first one agreed to, the contractor is not caught between a verbal yes and a written no, and an alternative method gets one accountable decision instead of a hallway conversation nobody can prove later.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats a verbal okay — from a plans examiner, an inspector, or the builder — as special permission. The definition is narrower: the written consent of the AHJ. No writing, no permission, however senior the person who nodded.
inspection_fails: Alternative method built on a verbal okay; the final inspector has no record of it and writes it up.
Work done first, written consent requested after — the AHJ declines, and the work comes out.
Builder's letter filed as 'special permission' — the consent never came from the AHJ.
Consent letter left at the office; nothing with the permit documents on site when the inspector asks.

sections.title: Garage, kitchen, and laundry area — how the Code uses area names
sections.plain_explanation:
Of these three area names, only one is a formal Article 100 definition:
• Kitchen: "an area with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation and cooking." Both halves must be present — a portable appliance plugged in on the counter does not create a kitchen.
• Garage: no standalone Article 100 definition in the 2020 Code. The Code uses the word in its rules — garage receptacles and their GFCI protection in 210.8(A)(2) and 210.52(G) — and it takes its ordinary meaning: the vehicle space and its attached unfinished areas.
• Laundry area: also no standalone definition. The laundry branch circuit is 210.11(C)(2) and laundry-area GFCI is 210.8(A)(10); the term means where laundry equipment is installed or intended to be.
Treat the kitchen test as a definition to apply exactly, and the other two as usage terms settled by the plan's intended use of the space.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks plan, the 'bonus room' over the garage shows a sink and a cooktop on the drawings. Both halves of the kitchen test are present, so wire it as a kitchen — its Chapter 2 circuit and GFCI rules follow the name. Same job, second change: the owner moves the laundry from the mud room to an upstairs closet after rough-in. The 210.11(C)(2) laundry circuit and the 210.8(A)(10) GFCI protection have to move with it. Settle every room's use before rough-in; a moved area after wiring is rework. The detailed area rules live in Article 210, covered in Chapter 2 of this book.
sections.sharma_note: S-08: the dryer circuit uses a Siemens Q230GF 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker, because NEC 2020 requires GFCI protection for receptacles in laundry areas, including 250V receptacles.
sections.figure_idea: House plan with garage, kitchen and laundry shaded in three colors, each tagged with the chapter that carries its main rules.
sections.why_it_exists: The room's name is a switch that turns whole rule sets on and off. Call a wet bar a kitchen and you owe small-appliance circuits and countertop GFCI it never needed. Miss a real kitchen, or a laundry that moved, and the required circuits and GFCI protection land in the wrong room — found at inspection, after the walls are closed.

Room with a sink and a permanent cooktop wired as a dining area — the kitchen definition was met and its Chapter 2 rules were missed.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'A room with a sink and a microwave on the counter is a kitchen.' It is not. The definition needs permanent provisions for food preparation and cooking; a portable appliance plugged in for the inspection does not create them. Both halves of the test, or it is not a kitchen.

sections.title: Article 110 — Requirements for electrical installations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 110 sets the general rules that apply to almost every installation: use approved and listed equipment the way its listing intends, terminate conductors correctly, do neat and workmanlike work, mark what needs marking, and leave safe working space around equipment. If a habit is wrong on every job, the rule against it is probably in this article.
• Approval and listing: equipment is approved (110.2) and installed and used the way its listing and labeling intend (110.3(B)). A breaker that merely fits the slot is not approved for the panel.
• Terminations: conductors land on terminals rated for the metal and tightened to the marking (110.14).
• Workmanship: neat and workmanlike, with covers and deadfronts in place (110.12).
• Working space: clear space in front of equipment that may be worked on energized — 3 ft deep at a 120/240 V house panel (110.26(A)).
• Identification: disconnecting means marked to show what they disconnect (110.22).
sections.on_the_job: Most Article 110 failures are visible without a meter: wrong-brand breakers, sloppy terminations, unmarked disconnects, blocked panels. A slow walk with this article in mind catches them before the inspector does. On a Sharma final walk in Marion Oaks that means Siemens breakers in the Siemens panel (new gear is Siemens), every disconnect labeled, and the 3 ft in front of the panel swept clear of the builder's paint cans before the inspector arrives.

sections.why_it_exists: Most electrical fires and shock injuries do not come from exotic code sections. They come from the basics that show up on every job: a loose lug heating for years, a wrong-brand breaker that was never tested in that panel, a panel nobody can reach in an emergency. Article 110 is where the Code parks those basics, which is why inspectors write it up more than almost anything else.

sections.title: Scope of Article 110
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 110 states the general requirements for electrical installations. It is the Code's ground floor: before any equipment article or wiring-method article adds its own rules, Article 110 sets the terms every installation has to meet.
• Approval and examination: equipment is approved (110.2), examined for suitability (110.3), and listed gear is installed and used by its instructions (110.3(B)).
• Ratings and fault duty: equipment is used at the voltage it is rated for (110.4), and its interrupting and short-circuit ratings have to suit the system (110.9, 110.10).
• Connections: conductors land on terminals suited to them, tightened to the specified torque (110.14, 110.14(D)).
• Marking and space: equipment is durably marked with its ratings (110.21), and access and working space are provided and kept clear around it (110.26).
• Two voltage worlds: Part II covers installations of 1000 volts, nominal, or less. Part III adds stricter rules for installations over 1000 volts (110.31).
The article is not limited to services or to panels. It follows equipment into every occupancy the later articles cover — houses, stores, factories, hospitals — and the specific articles then add their own rules on top of these. They do not replace them.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks new home, three rough-in questions are Article 110 questions, not house-article questions. Is the panel's interrupting rating enough for the fault current the utility can deliver (110.9)? Are the lugs torqued to the value printed on the panel label (110.14(D))? Is the working space — 30 in wide, 3 ft deep — taped out and kept clear in the garage (110.26(A))? Start in 110, then open the equipment's own article for whatever it adds.

sections.title: Approval of equipment and conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors and equipment required or permitted by the Code are acceptable only if approved. Approved is an Article 100 word: it means acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. In practice, approval is shown through listing and labeling by a qualified testing laboratory, and the four words of the family are not interchangeable:
• Approved — acceptable to the AHJ.
• Listed — the product appears in the testing organization's published list of products it has evaluated.
• Labeled — the testing organization has attached its label to the product.
• Identified — recognizable as suitable for the specific use in question.
Equipment with no path to approval does not become acceptable because it was cheap, available, or already on the truck. A product can be well made and still not be listed, and a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for that panel.
sections.on_the_job: Check approvals at order and delivery time, not at trim-out. The breaker question is settled before the truck rolls: Siemens gear for new work (S-02), and in an existing panel only the breakers listed for that panel — a Square D panel gets Square D breakers (S-03), even when another brand snaps in and 'works.' A non-listed substitute discovered at trim-out costs a return trip and can hold up the whole job.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 and S-03 keep Sharma inside this rule: Siemens gear for new work, and only breakers listed for the panel in existing panels.

sections.why_it_exists: Listing is the evidence that a product was tested against the hazards it will meet — heat, fault current, flame, and how it behaves when it fails. Unapproved gear has no evaluated failure story, so when it lets go, it lets go as a surprise: the breaker that never trips, the driver that cooks in a closed ceiling. AHJ acceptance is also the practical gate to a passed inspection and an energized building.

sections.title: Examination, identification, installation, and use of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
110.3(A) lists what is weighed when equipment is examined and judged for an installation:
• Suitability for the installation and use.
• Mechanical strength and durability.
• Wire-bending space and connection space for its conductors.
• Electrical insulation.
• Heating effects.
• Arcing effects.
• Classification by type, size, voltage, current capacity and specific use.
In plain terms: the right equipment, of the right rating, in the right place, with room for its conductors to land properly. 110.3(B) then requires listed or labeled equipment to be installed and used in accordance with its instructions, and 110.3(C) covers listing of equipment by a qualified electrical testing laboratory where the Code requires it. Suitability is judged before the gear goes in — not after the inspector arrives.
sections.on_the_job: Suitability is decided before installation. On a Lake County pool job, the replacement pump motor that came out of the box was an open drip-proof motor meant for a dry location; the equipment pad sits out in the weather beside the pool. It never got wired — the motor that went in is identified for the location. A device rated for a dry interior wall does not become suitable on an exterior wet wall because it was the one in the box.

nec2023_change.change: Cybersecurity for networked life safety equipment joined the list of things weighed when judging equipment, and gear identified for a use now has to be installed and used by its instructions too. New 110.3(A)(8): approving networked life safety gear now means weighing its cybersecurity, so it holds up against hacking and unauthorized updates and keeps working safely.

sections.title: Install and use listed equipment per its instructions
sections.plain_explanation:
Listed or labeled equipment must be installed and used in accordance with the instructions included in its listing or labeling. The manufacturer's instructions are not suggestions where the listing depends on them:
• A torque value in the instructions is a requirement. 110.14(D) sends you back to it, with a torque tool in hand.
• A conductor-material marking — copper only, or CU-AL — limits what may land on the terminal.
• A temperature marking works with the termination rules of 110.14(C): sizing starts from the 60 °C column, or the 75 °C column where the equipment is listed and marked for it.
• A mounting requirement — orientation, clearance, enclosure type — is part of the listing, not a preference.
If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks trim-out, the door label of the Siemens panel gives the lug torque table and marks the terminations 75 °C. The apprentice torques the feeder lugs to the printed value with a torque wrench and lands the conductors the label allows. The same panel closed up 'hand tight by feel' is the call-back Sharma takes six months later: a hot lug and a nuisance-tripped main. Read the label inside the panel door, the sheet in the device box, and the nameplate on the equipment. If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.

sections.title: Voltages
sections.plain_explanation:
The voltage the Code means is the nominal system voltage — the voltage the circuit actually operates at — unless a rule says otherwise. Equipment's voltage rating may not be less than the nominal voltage of the circuit it is connected to, and a device rated for a lower voltage does not become suitable on a higher-voltage circuit just because its terminals fit. Load, protection and clearance rules are all keyed to that nominal voltage.
Common nominal system voltages (the list itself is in 220.5(A), not in 110.4):
• 120 V — single-phase branch circuits
• 120/240 V — the standard one-family house service
• 208Y/120 V — three-phase wye, common in commercial buildings and multifamily services
• 240 V — single-phase or three-phase delta
• 277 V — one leg of a 480Y/277 V system to neutral, the commercial lighting voltage
• 480Y/277 V and 480 V — larger commercial services
A device marked for one system voltage is not interchangeable with another just because the plugs look alike.
sections.on_the_job: On a strip-plaza retrofit in Kissimmee, the existing lighting runs at 277 V from a 480Y/277 V service. The replacement drivers the supplier shipped are marked 120 V only. They fit the same boxes and land on the same wires — and they cannot go in. The crew holds that part of the job at the supply-house counter: 277 V drivers, or a different fixture. The nameplate gets checked against the system in front of you — 120/240 V single-phase, 208Y/120 V and 480Y/277 V three-phase are different worlds for device ratings, even when the hardware looks similar.

sections.why_it_exists: A voltage rating is a safety rating, not a suggestion. Put a device on a higher voltage than it is marked for and its insulation, its contact gaps and its ability to interrupt an arc are all undersized for the fault it may have to break. The nominal-voltage rule also keeps everyone's math on the same page: loads, protection and clearances are figured from the name of the system, not from whatever the meter reads that afternoon.

Section 110.4 keys the rule to the nominal voltage of the circuit, and equipment may not be rated below it. The mirror-image trap is hunting for the list of system voltages in 110.4: the list lives in 220.5(A).

sections.title: Conductors — general
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors in the Code are copper unless a rule or an equipment marking provides for another metal. Where other materials such as aluminum or copper-clad aluminum are used, the sizes in the Code's tables and rules are read in the column and on the terms for that material. The metal of the conductor is part of the design, not an afterthought at the supply house.
• Table 310.16 has two column families: copper on the left; aluminum and copper-clad aluminum sharing the right-hand columns.
• Same size, different metal, different answer: 12 AWG at 75 °C is 25 A in copper and 20 A in aluminum or CCA.
• The breaker caps follow the metal too (240.4(D)): 12 AWG copper is capped at 20 A; 12 AWG aluminum or CCA at 15 A.
• Terminations must be marked for the metal landed on them (110.14).
sections.on_the_job: Service change on a Marion Oaks house: the underground lateral is aluminum, the branch circuits are copper, and each metal gets read in its own column before anything is ordered. Where CCA goes in on a Sharma house, S-10 sets the pattern — one AWG size larger than the copper it replaces: 12 AWG CCA on a 15 A circuit, 10 AWG CCA on a 20 A circuit, landed only on terminations marked for it and never backstabbed. If the spool on the truck is not the metal the takeoff assumed, the sizing starts over.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: copper is Sharma's default. When CCA is used, size one AWG larger, use the aluminum column of Table 310.16, land it only on terminations listed for it, and never backstab.

sections.why_it_exists: Aluminum and CCA carry less current at the same size, and they behave differently under a screw: they creep, they oxidize, and they work loose in terminations that were only tested for copper. Read the copper column for an aluminum conductor and you build a hot spot into every lug on the run. The metal is not a purchasing detail — it is half of the ampacity answer.

CCA backstabbed into receptacle push-in terminals — copper only, and Sharma never backstabs (S-10).

In aluminum or CCA, 12 AWG is worth 20 A at 75 °C in the table and is capped at a 15 A breaker. The exam expects one question before any ampacity answer: which metal?

sections.title: Conductor sizes — AWG and circular mils
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductor sizes are expressed in American Wire Gauge (AWG) for the smaller sizes and in circular mil area for the larger ones. Above 4/0 AWG, the kcmil number is the area in thousands of circular mils: 500 kcmil is 500,000 circular mils.
The size designation is a standard language — the same AWG number means the same conductor size whoever made the cable.
Size by itself is not ampacity. The rating still comes from the ampacity tables, the termination limits and the conditions of use.
The circular-mil areas in the table are what the proportional upsizing rules work from: when ungrounded conductors are upsized, the equipment grounding conductor is upsized by the ratio of these numbers (250.122).
sections.on_the_job: Long run from a Marion Oaks house panel to a detached garage: voltage drop pushes the ungrounded conductors from 12 AWG up to 10 AWG. The grounding conductor goes up by the same ratio — 10,380 ÷ 6,530 is about 1.59, and 6,530 × 1.59 lands on 10,380, so the 12 AWG equipment grounding conductor becomes a 10 AWG (250.122). Speak sizes in AWG up through 4/0 and in kcmil above that, and never let a breaker handle rating substitute for the ampacity check behind it.
sections.why_it_exists: Crews who treat size as a rating get both directions wrong: a fat conductor read on the wrong table column still overheats, and a grounding conductor left small after an upsize becomes the weak link in the fault path. The areas look like trivia until a voltage-drop upsize turns them into a ratio you have to run.
inspection_fails: Equipment grounding conductor left at 12 AWG after the ungrounded conductors were upsized to 10 AWG for voltage drop — the 250.122 proportional increase was missed.
12 AWG conductors protected at 30 A — the size was treated as the ampacity instead of checking the tables (240.4(D)).
Panel schedule rejected: feeder sizes above 4/0 written in AWG instead of kcmil.

sections.title: Wiring integrity
sections.plain_explanation:
Completed wiring installations must be free from three things:
• Short circuits — conductors touching that should never touch.
• Ground faults — a live conductor connected to ground or to grounded metal by a path that is not supposed to exist.
• Any connection to ground other than the ones the Code requires or permits — the grounded conductor meets ground where the Code says, and nowhere else.
That is the whole rule of 110.7, and it is why continuity and insulation checks happen before energizing: the installation has to be proven clean, not assumed clean. Do not confuse it with equipment integrity. The rule that internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other parts must not be damaged or contaminated lives at 110.12(B), not here. Section 110.7 is about the wiring; 110.12(B) is about the gear.
sections.on_the_job: Before you energize, prove the install: no shorts, no ground faults, no stray grounds. On a final check at an Ocala house, our continuity test caught a dead short on a 20 A kitchen circuit before the panel was ever made hot — a drywall screw had pierced the run behind the cabinets. Twenty minutes with the meter; the same fault found after energizing would have meant a tripping breaker, a callback, and a finished wall opened on warranty. If the gear itself is damaged or contaminated inside, that is a 110.12(B) problem — a different section, with the same stop-and-fix answer.
sections.why_it_exists: A short or a ground fault that nobody finds on test day gets found by the breaker, by an arc, or by the person who touches the metal — at full fault current, with the building occupied. Testing before energizing is the cheap moment to catch a nicked conductor or a stray ground connection. After energizing, the same defect is a fire investigation or a shock injury.
sections.exam_trap: The exam trap is 110.12(B) dressed as 110.7. A question describes damaged busbars or contaminated internal parts and offers 110.7 as the answer — wrong section; that is equipment integrity at 110.12(B). Section 110.7 covers the completed wiring only: free from short circuits, ground faults, and connections to ground that the Code does not require or permit.

sections.title: Wiring methods — use only recognized methods
sections.plain_explanation:
Only wiring methods the Code recognizes for the application may be used. A cable or raceway that conducts electricity is not thereby a permitted wiring method for a given location: each method has its own article, its permitted uses and its prohibited uses, and those govern.
• NM cable — Article 334. EMT — Article 358. PVC conduit — Article 352. MC cable — Article 330. AC cable — Article 320. Rigid metal conduit — Article 344.
• The article's limits decide the locations: indoors, outdoors, wet, concealed, exposed.
• Improvised assemblies and products used outside their article's limits fail here before any other rule is reached.
sections.on_the_job: Before running anything, name the method and its article — NM cable, EMT, PVC, MC and the rest each carry their own use lists. A method allowed indoors is not automatically allowed outdoors or in a wet location. On a detached-garage feed in Clermont, that means the decision happens before the material list: NM inside the house walls, a method whose article permits the underground run, and a method permitted exposed on the garage's block wall. Name the method first and the rough-in survives inspection.

That reaches wiring outside buildings too. A recognized wiring method can go in any type of building, occupancy or premises wiring system, unless another rule says otherwise.

sections.title: Interrupting rating
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment meant to interrupt current during a fault has to be able to interrupt the fault current that can actually be delivered at its terminals. A breaker asked to open a fault beyond its interrupting rating can fail violently instead of clearing the fault. The rating is printed on the device and must equal or exceed the available fault current at that point.
Two companion rules travel with it:
• 110.10: the whole circuit — overcurrent devices, total impedance and the short-circuit current ratings of the components — must work together so a fault clears without extensive damage.
• 110.24: at service equipment in other than dwelling units, the available fault current is field-marked on the equipment, with the date the calculation was made.
sections.on_the_job: Check the kAIC marking on breakers against the job's available fault current, especially close to large services and transformers. Worked example from a small commercial service: the fault-current calculation comes back at 22 kA. A panel filled with 10 kAIC breakers is under-rated gear — every one of those breakers is being asked to open a fault more than twice its rating. Breakers marked 22 kAIC meet the number exactly; 65 kAIC gear covers it with room for the utility's next transformer change. Series-rated combinations are only valid as tested and documented combinations, not as a field guess. Sharma standard is Siemens on new gear — read the kAIC on the label before the gear is set, not at trim-out.

nec2023_change.change: A wording update using the defined term available fault current. Every breaker and fuse still has to be rated to interrupt the available fault current at its line terminals. Any breaker or fuse meant to open fault current needs an interrupting rating that meets or beats the available fault current at its line terminals.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.9 Interrupting rating

sections.why_it_exists: A breaker that tries to open a fault beyond its rating can weld its contacts, rupture, or keep feeding the arc — the fault burns on instead of clearing. And available fault current is not fixed: when the utility swaps in a bigger transformer, the same panel can become under-rated without anyone on site touching it.
inspection_fails: 10 kAIC breakers installed where the available fault current is 22 kA — under-rated equipment (110.9).
Series-rated combination installed without the tested, documented pairing and its labels.
No available-fault-current marking at a commercial service — or the marking never updated after a utility transformer change (110.24).
Replacement breaker of a different type with a lower interrupting rating swapped in during a repair.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is mixing up the two ratings on the breaker. A 200 A breaker is not 'stronger' against faults than a 100 A breaker — the amp rating is the load rating. The interrupting rating is the kAIC number, and a little 20 A breaker can carry 65 kAIC while a big frame breaker carries only 10 kAIC.

sections.title: Circuit impedance and fault-current performance
sections.plain_explanation:
110.10 is the performance rule standing behind the rating rules. The overcurrent devices, the total impedance of the circuit, and the other components of the circuit must be selected and coordinated so that, under a short circuit or ground fault, the fault is cleared without extensive damage to the equipment in the circuit.
• The fault loop has to be a low-impedance path: conductors, raceway, bonding and grounding connections tight enough that a fault draws current high enough to open the device fast. A high-impedance loop can leave a fault arcing at a current too low to trip anything.
• Every device that has to open the fault needs an interrupting rating at least equal to the available fault current at its terminals (110.9).
• Every component in the circuit needs a short-circuit current rating that suits the system it is part of — it can only be asked to withstand the fault energy the circuit can actually deliver.
No single part passes or fails alone. 110.10 judges the circuit as a team.
sections.on_the_job: Small commercial tenant build-out in Ocala: the utility's fault-current letter for the new 400 A service states an available fault current of 22,000 A. The specified Siemens panelboard carries a 22 kA short-circuit current rating and its breakers are rated 22 kA interrupting, so the team matches the system. The value-brand panel the GC tried to substitute was marked 10 kA; under 110.9 and 110.10 it cannot go in, however good the price. The available fault current is field-marked on the service equipment with the date the calculation was made (110.24).

sections.why_it_exists: A fault is the highest-energy event a circuit ever sees. If the loop impedance is too high, the breaker never trips and the fault burns until something melts open. If a component's rating is too low, it can rupture instead of opening. The rule exists so a fault ends as a trip — not a fire, and not an explosion.
inspection_fails: Breakers with an interrupting rating below the available fault current at their line terminals (110.9, 110.10).
Panelboard or equipment short-circuit current rating below the available fault current — the nameplate never checked against the utility's number.
Loose, corroded or painted bonding and grounding connections raising the fault-loop impedance until a ground fault cannot clear.
Available fault current not field-marked at the service, or the marking left stale after a utility change raised it (110.24).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'the breaker is rated 22 kA, so the installation complies.' 110.10 is wider than any one device. A correctly rated breaker on a high-impedance fault loop still fails the section, because the fault never clears — impedance and every component's withstand rating count too.

sections.title: Deteriorating agents
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment must not sit in conditions that will destroy it. Unless equipment is identified for the operating environment, it does not go where it will be exposed to:
• Damp or wet locations.
• Gases, fumes, vapors, liquids, or other agents that have a deteriorating effect on the equipment or the conductors.
• Excessive temperatures.
Ordinary equipment in a corrosive or wet environment fails early, and it can fail dangerously. The answer is not paint or tape; the answer is equipment identified for that environment, which in practice means the enclosure type marked on the gear. The types Sharma meets most, from 110.28:
• Type 1 — indoor, general purpose.
• Type 3R — outdoor and rainproof; the standard house disconnect and meter enclosure.
• Type 4 — watertight, even against hose-directed water.
• Type 4X — Type 4 performance plus corrosion resistance, for washdown and coastal work.
• Type 12 — indoor industrial, against dust and dripping noncorrosive liquids.
sections.on_the_job: Coastal Florida is the standing test case. On a service call at a beachside house in Brevard County, the disconnect on the ocean-side wall was rusted through at the bottom seam after a few salt-air seasons, with green corrosion on the lugs. That is a replacement, not a cleanup: Type 3R minimum outside, and Type 4X where hose water or pool chemicals join the salt. In the pool equipment room at the same house, chlorine stored beside the panel had done the same work through the air. Identify the environment first, then pick equipment identified for it.
sections.florida_note: Salt air along Florida coasts is a deteriorating agent. Exterior and coastal gear needs to be identified for the exposure, and corrosion found at service calls should be reported, not just wiped off.

sections.why_it_exists: Corrosion does not stop at the cabinet skin. It eats lugs and terminations, raises resistance at every joint, and turns a sound connection into a heater. Moisture and chemical vapor work the same way from the inside, attacking insulation and bus. Gear that rots in place fails years early, and the failure is usually heat or a ground fault, not a clean shutdown.

Standard indoor equipment in a fertilizer storage room or a car wash bay, attacked by chemical vapor and hose-directed water (110.11).
Equipment mounted where excessive temperatures were never accounted for, with no check that it is identified for the heat (110.11).
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating identification as a coating: spray it with rust-proof paint and call it identified for the coast. Identification is the manufacturer's rating, shown by the type marked on the enclosure. Paint does not turn a Type 1 box into a Type 4X, and a stainless look does not either. If the marked type does not cover the exposure, the equipment does not belong there.

sections.title: Mechanical execution of work — workmanship and unused openings
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrical work has to be done in a neat and workmanlike manner — that is a code rule, not a compliment. It covers how the whole job is put together:
• Unused openings in enclosures, boxes and equipment must be closed with closures that give protection much like the wall of the equipment itself. A missing knockout blank is an open door for fingers, pests and arc products.
• Conductors must be protected where their insulation can be damaged.
• 110.12(B) covers integrity of equipment and connections: internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals and other components must not be damaged or contaminated by foreign materials, and there must be no damaged, broken, bent, cut or deteriorated parts.
Keeping water out of enclosures in wet locations is a different rule — see 312.2 and 314.15 — not part of 110.12.
sections.on_the_job: On a garage panel in a new Marion Oaks house, close every unused opening with a listed blank or plug the day the gear is set — not tape, and not a folded piece of can. On exterior Florida gear the same open hole is also a pest and water entry, so it does not wait for trim-out. Neat work is not cosmetic here: 110.12 is the section the inspector cites when a panel looks like a hazard before he has tested a single thing.

An open knockout lets a finger, a lizard or a nest reach live parts, and in a fault it vents arc products straight out of the box. Paint, drywall dust and bent or damaged parts inside equipment raise resistance, trap heat and hide the defect until it fails under load — usually on the hottest afternoon of the year.

It is a code requirement with teeth: an unused opening closed with tape fails, and paint or drywall dust on the busbars is a 110.12(B) violation, not a cleanup note.

sections.title: Mounting and cooling of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment has to be firmly secured to its mounting surface, and it must not be mounted in a way that blocks the cooling it was designed for. Section 110.13 states the two duties separately:
• Mounting — 110.13(A): equipment must be firmly secured to the mounting surface. Wooden plugs driven into masonry, concrete or plaster are not an acceptable way to secure equipment.
• Cooling — 110.13(B): equipment that depends on the natural circulation of air must not be installed so the airflow over its cooling surfaces is prevented. It cannot be buried in insulation or boxed in tight.
Where the manufacturer's instructions set spacing the equipment needs to breathe, those instructions carry Code force through 110.3(B).
sections.on_the_job: Anchor gear with real fasteners into structure or masonry anchors, keep vents and fins clear, and check that a recessed installation still lets the equipment breathe as its instructions require. On a block garage wall that means sleeve or wedge anchors into the block — never a wooden plug — and no boxes stored against a dry-type transformer's fins.
sections.why_it_exists: Loose gear vibrates, works its terminations loose, and can pull against its raceways. Overheated gear cooks its insulation and electronics and fails years early — or becomes the ignition source itself. Florida garages and attics run hot to begin with, so the cooling margin the manufacturer designed in is not spare capacity to spend on storage and insulation.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps live on this page. A wooden plug in a masonry wall can feel solid, so it must be fine — 110.13(A) names it as not permitted for securing equipment. And equipment that physically fits in a tight box must be allowed to run in one — if it cools by natural air circulation, boxing it in defeats the design and fails 110.13(B).

Equipment loose on its anchors, rocking when the raceway is pulled.

sections.title: Electrical connections — terminations in general
sections.plain_explanation:
Most electrical failures start at a connection, and this section is the Code's main defense. Conductors must land on terminals suited to their metal and size, with the connection made by an approved method.
• Terminals and splices must be identified for the conductor material — read the lug or device marking before the wire goes in (110.14(A)).
• Dissimilar metals in contact may be joined only where the device is identified for that combination. Corrosion between unlike metals loosens and overheats a joint over time.
• Solder, where used, cannot be the thing that holds a joint together. A soldered splice must first be mechanically and electrically secure without solder (110.14(B)).
• Copper and CCA are not dissimilar metals. Aluminum with copper, or aluminum with CCA, is the dissimilar pair (Sharma S-10).
sections.on_the_job: Read the lug and device markings before landing wire. CU-only means copper only. A connector for aluminum, copper and CCA together must carry the AL-CU or CU-AL marking, or the intermixed marking where the metals actually touch, and breaker and equipment lugs get the same check. On a Marion Oaks rough-in with a new 200 A Siemens panel, the check runs at every landing point: 15 A and 20 A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise, but devices 30 A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU (S-10).
sections.sharma_note: S-10 CCA practice: 15A and 20A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise; devices 30A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU. Copper and CCA are not dissimilar metals; aluminum with copper, or aluminum with CCA, is. Backstab (push-in) terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only — never backstab CCA, stranded wire, or 12 AWG. UNVERIFIED FLAG (v1 README item 9): the UL guide wording behind the CCA terminal markings (RTRT / WJQR / ZMVV / AALZ) was taken from NEMA and UL/IAEI quotations, not read first-hand in UL Product iQ, and no CC or CC/CU marking was found in the ZMVV table. Do not invent a marking. A NEMA citation to 404.15(C) for switch terminals was not checked against the code text and is not relied on here.

sections.why_it_exists: A connection is the one place current has to pass from one piece of metal to another. Let the wrong metals corrode against each other, or let solder alone carry the joint, and resistance climbs. The joint heats, the heat loosens it further, and the end of that road is a glowing connection, arcing, and a fire inside a box or a panel — usually years after the installer has left.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer says copper and CCA are dissimilar metals that may never touch. They are not a dissimilar pair, and they may be intermixed where the device allows it. The pairs that need a device identified for the combination are aluminum with copper and aluminum with CCA.

sections.title: Temperature limits at terminations
sections.plain_explanation:
A termination is the lug or terminal where a conductor lands. The conductor's insulation may be rated 90 °C, but the ampacity you may use is capped by the temperature rating of the terminations at both ends of the run.
• Circuits of 100 A or less, or conductors 14 through 1 AWG: use the 60 °C column of Table 310.16, unless the equipment is listed and marked for a higher temperature.
• Circuits over 100 A, or conductors larger than 1 AWG: use the 75 °C column, unless the equipment is listed and marked otherwise.
• The temperature rating of a conductor cannot be used above the lowest temperature rating of any termination it lands on. One 60 °C lug holds the whole run to 60 °C.
• The 90 °C column still earns its keep: it is the starting point for temperature correction and conductor-count adjustment under 310.15. The final ampacity still cannot beat the termination column.
sections.on_the_job: A 200 A feeder on a small commercial job in Marion Oaks — Siemens panelboard, tenant space — run in 3/0 AWG THHN copper. The 90 °C column rates 3/0 at 225 A, but both ends land on 75 °C lugs, so the feeder sizes from the 75 °C column: 200 A, exactly the feeder rating. The first pick, 2/0, reads 195 A at 90 °C — tempting, but only 175 A at 75 °C, short of 200 A. Commercial on purpose: 310.12 sizes dwelling services and feeders on its own table, where 2/0 copper is a legal 200 A dwelling service. Same rule at the small end: 12 AWG THHN on a 20 A breaker starts at 30 A in the 90 °C column for correction math, but at the breaker the circuit is a 60 °C, 20 A circuit.
sections.figure_idea: A conductor run drawn as a chain — wire rated 90, breaker lug rated 75, equipment lug rated 60 — with the whole chain sized at the weakest link, 60.
sections.why_it_exists: The lug is the weak point of the run. Insulation along the conductor sheds heat into the air, but at the terminal the heat is trapped in a small mass of metal bolted to a breaker or switch that was tested at 60 °C or 75 °C. Land a conductor at its 90 °C ampacity on a 60 °C lug and the terminal overheats first: nuisance trips, insulation cooked back from the lug, and a connection that loosens into a high-resistance fault.
sections.exam_trap: The classic trap: 'THHN is rated 90 °C, so 12 AWG THHN can be protected at 30 A.' Wrong twice. 110.14(C) holds a circuit of 100 A or less to the 60 °C column — 20 A for 12 AWG copper — unless the equipment is marked for 75 °C, and 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A anyway. The 90 °C column is for correction and adjustment math, not for picking the breaker.

sections.title: Torque — tighten to the specified value
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a manufacturer gives a torque value for a terminal, the connection has to be tightened to that value using an approved means, unless the equipment has been tested and marked so another method is known to give the same result.
• The approved means is a calibrated torque tool — a torque wrench or torque screwdriver — or a device such as a shear bolt or breakaway fastener that shows the proper torque was reached.
• The specified torque is normally printed on the equipment label or in its instructions. Those instructions carry Code force under 110.3(B).
• Hand-tight by feel is not a value. Two installers' 'tight' can differ by half.
• If no value is indicated, contact the manufacturer. In the absence of a manufacturer's value, Annex I of UL 486A-486B — reprinted as NEC Informative Annex I — gives torque values by screw and conductor size.
sections.on_the_job: New 200 A Siemens panel on a slab home in Ocala: the torque table is printed on the label inside the door — main lugs, neutral bar and breaker terminals each carry their own value. The torque screwdriver handles the small breaker and device terminals; the main lugs take a torque wrench. Keep both on the truck, use the label value for every lug at trim and service work, and re-check after landing all conductors — a lug torqued before the last conductor went in is not finished. Existing checklist item SP-15 covers the field routine.

sections.why_it_exists: A loose terminal is a resistor. Current through a high-resistance joint makes heat, the heat cycles loosen the joint further, and the end of that road is arcing, a burned lug, or a fire inside the panel. Too tight is its own failure: crushed strands, a cracked lug, or a screw that snaps later. The specified value is the one the equipment was tested at — that is why the Code makes it a rule instead of a suggestion.

Main lugs run down with an impact driver until the tool 'sounded right.'
Label torque table ignored; generic values used even though the manufacturer printed its own.
Conductor strands crushed and splayed from over-torque, lug cracked at the barrel.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'gudentight' — snug plus a quarter turn. 110.14(D) wants the indicated value, reached with an approved means. The second trap is reaching for the Annex I fallback values when the equipment label prints a value: the manufacturer's number governs, and the fallback exists only for when no value is given.

sections.title: High-leg marking on 4-wire delta systems
sections.plain_explanation:
On a 4-wire, 3-phase delta system where the midpoint of one phase winding is used as a circuit conductor — the common 240/120 V delta — the voltages to ground are not equal:
• Two legs sit at 120 V to ground.
• The third leg — the high leg — sits at 208 V to ground.
110.15 requires that high-leg conductor to be durably and permanently marked by an orange finish, or identified by other effective means, at each point on the system where a connection is made if the grounded conductor is also present. The marking is what keeps a 120 V load from being landed on the leg that sits at 208 V to ground.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets high legs on older light-commercial services. Before landing any 120 V circuit in a delta panel, identify which leg is the high leg, confirm it is orange-marked, and keep 120 V loads off it. On a panel change at a small warehouse, the crew meters every leg to ground before landing anything: A reads 120 V, B reads 208 V, C reads 120 V — B is the high leg. It gets its orange identification at the panel and at the disconnect, the 120 V lighting and receptacle circuits land on A and C only, and the panel schedule is marked so the next electrician sees it before he meters.
sections.figure_idea: A delta panel schedule with the B phase column shaded orange and the voltage-to-ground values 120 / 208 / 120 written under the three legs.
sections.why_it_exists: A 120 V load landed on the high leg sees 208 V to ground and burns up — controls, ballasts and electronics die, and equipment can be energized in ways nobody expects. A delta panel looks like any other panel from the front; the only thing standing between a tired apprentice and a fried control board is the orange identification on the odd leg. That is why the marking has to be durable and permanent, not a scrap of tape that falls off by trim-out.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer marks the high leg with whatever tape is in the truck, or assumes a 120 V load can share the high leg because “it is still just one phase.” 110.15 requires an orange finish or other effective means, and the 208 V-to-ground leg feeds only loads rated for it.

sections.title: Arc-flash hazard warning marking
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment that is likely to be examined, adjusted, serviced or maintained while energized — such as switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers in other than dwelling settings — must carry a durable, field-applied warning marking about the arc-flash hazard:
• 110.16(A) is the warning marking itself. It warns the person approaching the gear; it does not replace safe work practice, and it belongs where that person will see it before anything is opened.
• 110.16(B): in other than dwelling units, service equipment rated 1200A or more also needs a permanent label meeting 110.21(B). The label shows the nominal system voltage, the available fault current at the service overcurrent devices, the clearing time of those devices based on that fault current, and the date the label was applied. It is not required where an arc-flash label is applied per acceptable industry practice.
sections.on_the_job: On a small commercial job — a 1600A, 480Y/277 V service for an Ocala retail plaza — the (B) label is filled in from the fault-current figures before final: nominal voltage, the available fault current at the service devices, their clearing time at that current, and the date it went on. Confirm the general arc-flash warning is present and legible before you call final. Houses are not the target of this section, but the hazard it names is real on any energized panel.

sections.why_it_exists: Arc flash is the hazard you cannot see coming: opening a dead-front over a faulted or miswired bus can release an arc blast before a hand can pull back. The warning makes the next person stop, suit up and plan before the cover comes off — and the (B) label puts the numbers that drive the safety decisions on the gear itself, where they are still needed ten years later.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps. First: “Once the label is on, the gear is protected.” The marking only warns — PPE and safe work practice still do the protecting. Second, the 2023 answer on a 2020 exam: 1000A and feeder-supplied equipment. Under NEC 2020, (B) covers service equipment rated 1200A or more; the wider 2023 net is labeled in the edition box and does not apply yet.

sections.title: Servicing and maintenance of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Start with the edition: this section does not exist in NEC 2020, the edition Florida enforces today. 110.17 is new in NEC 2023, and it sets the rules for servicing and maintaining electrical equipment:
• Servicing and maintenance are done by qualified persons. Experience alone is not the standard — the person doing the work needs the training and knowledge the task and its hazards require.
• The work is done per the manufacturer's instructions or listing information, industry standards, or as approved by the AHJ.
• Replacement parts and components must be suitable for the equipment: identified for it, from the original manufacturer, designed by an engineer experienced in replacement parts for that equipment, or approved by the AHJ.
sections.on_the_job: On service calls, Sharma already works this way: replace a failed component with the part identified for that equipment — the breaker type the Siemens panel is listed for, not one that happens to fit the stab. Treat unfamiliar gear, especially commercial switchgear, as a qualified-persons-only job until the right person is on it. On Florida permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026, this section is not yet the enforced text; it becomes the rule with the FBC 9th Ed. for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.
sections.florida_note: Not in force on Florida jobs under NEC 2020 (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026); know it for the NEC 2023 exam. FBC 9th Ed. (NEC 2023) applies to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.

sections.why_it_exists: Equipment gets serviced for decades after the install crew leaves. A will-fit part that almost matches, or a helper set loose on gear he was never trained on, turns a repair into the next failure — a lug that overheats, a breaker that will not trip, a fault nobody can clear. The rule ties the work to trained people and identified parts so a repair restores the equipment instead of quietly changing it.
sections.exam_trap: Two trap answers. First: “He has twenty years in the trade, so he is qualified to service anything.” The section measures training and knowledge for the task and its hazards, not years. Second: “A replacement part that physically fits is suitable.” It is not — unless it is identified for the equipment or comes through the original manufacturer, an experienced engineer, or the AHJ.

sections.title: Arcing parts
sections.plain_explanation:
Some parts of electrical equipment arc in normal operation. Switch and breaker contacts open under load, contactors pull in and drop out, motor brushes ride a commutator — arcs, sparks, and sometimes molten metal are part of how the equipment works. 110.18 does not try to ban the arc. It controls where the arc may happen:
• Parts that in ordinary operation produce arcs, sparks, flames, or molten metal must be enclosed, or separated and isolated from all combustible material.
• An arc inside properly enclosed equipment is expected, and contained.
• The same arcing part sitting open near material that can ignite is a fire waiting for its fuel.
There is no distance in inches in this section. The test is a condition: enclosed, or separated and isolated.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call in a Marion Oaks garage, the pattern is familiar: a contactor or an old open switch with its cover long gone, cycling a load, with paint cans and cardboard stacked against the same wall. Keep enclosures intact around switching equipment. Put the cover back or replace the device, move the storage off the gear, and flag arcing or sparking equipment found open or mounted tight against combustible storage for correction before you leave.

sections.why_it_exists: Every switching operation throws a small, very hot plasma event. Inside an enclosure it dies against metal. In the open — next to cardboard, paint, solvents, or stored household goods — it is an ignition source that fires on a schedule, every time the equipment cycles. Florida garages and storage rooms put the fuel and the arcing parts within the same few feet, which is exactly the pairing this rule breaks up.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is hunting for a number: 'how many inches from combustibles does 110.18 require?' It gives none — the rule is a condition, not a dimension. The second trap is calling arcing parts defects by themselves. They are normal in switching equipment; the violation is leaving them open to fuel, not the arc itself.

sections.title: Light and power from railway conductors (orientation)
sections.plain_explanation:
110.19 draws one hard line: circuits for lighting and power shall not be connected to any system that contains trolley wires with a ground return.
• The ban is on the connection itself, not on the voltage. A ground-return trolley system carries its return current through the rails and the earth, and a building's lighting and power circuits must never be tied into that.
• One exception: the connection is permitted in car houses, power houses, and passenger and freight stations operated in connection with electric railways — the railway's own buildings, run by the railway.
• Nothing else in premises wiring uses this section. Railway power installations themselves sit largely outside the Code's scope (90.2). The page is in the book so the numbering of Article 110 reads complete, not as a working rule.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma does not design or install railway power, so the field case is a request, not an installation: on a commercial job near a rail corridor, someone proposes feeding site lighting or a temporary circuit from 'railway power' because it is close. The answer is the one this page exists for — stop and escalate. Temporary power comes from the premises service under the ordinary rules, engineered work stays engineered, and no Sharma circuit connects to a trolley ground-return system.

sections.why_it_exists: A ground return puts traction current in the earth and in every buried metal path it can find. Tie a building system into that and you import stray current, shock exposure, and electrolytic corrosion of piping and conductors. The rule keeps two incompatible systems apart, and the exception stays inside buildings the railway itself operates, where the railway's own engineering controls both sides.

It bans the connection to a ground-return trolley system outright, and the only exception is inside the railway's own car houses, power houses, and stations — not in any building that happens to stand near tracks.

sections.title: Reconditioned equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
There is no 110.20 in NEC 2020 — this section is new in the 2023 NEC. Under the 2020 book, the only general reconditioned-equipment rule is the marking rule in 110.21(A)(2), plus scattered article rules such as 240.62 and 240.88.
What the 2023 section adds, for permits under the FBC 9th Ed.:
• It governs equipment that has been reconditioned — rebuilt or restored — as distinct from equipment that has merely been serviced or had a failed part replaced with an approved equal.
• Reconditioned equipment has to be evaluated and accepted under the section's terms, and the party that reconditioned it has to be identifiable.
• Some categories of equipment are restricted, or not permitted to be reconditioned at all.
• A previous listing does not automatically survive an extensive rebuild.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial renovations, treat refurbished switchboards, panelboards and breakers as a question, not a bargain: who reconditioned it, under what evaluation, and is that category of equipment permitted to be reconditioned? Get the answer before it is set, not at inspection. On a tenant build-out, a 400 A refurbished switchboard is not set until the reconditioner's name and date are read off the gear and the evaluation paperwork is in the job file; on today's 2020 permits, the 110.21(A)(2) marking is the first thing to check and the AHJ has the final say.

nec2023_change.change: New section: reconditioned equipment is allowed unless another rule bans it, and it gets accepted through a listing, a field label, the original maker's instructions, or approval by the authority having jurisdiction. sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating "reconditioned" and "serviced" as the same word. Swapping a failed breaker for an approved equal is service; a breaker that has been opened, rebuilt and restored is reconditioned, and it carries marking and acceptance duties. The second trap: assuming the original listing survives any rebuild. It does not.

sections.title: Marking — manufacturer marks and field-applied hazard marks
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment carries the manufacturer's name and its ratings so the user can tell what it is and what it is rated for.
• Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it has to be durable enough for its environment, use signal wording everyone recognizes, and not be handwritten where the Code requires a proper marking.
• A faded or missing rating plate makes equipment hard to approve and harder to service safely.
• Reconditioned equipment has its own marking rule at 110.21(A)(2): it must be marked with the name or trademark of the business that reconditioned it and the date of reconditioning, identified as reconditioned, and the original listing mark must be removed or voided — reconditioned gear is never passed off as new.
sections.on_the_job: Do not paint over, cover or discard rating labels. When you add a required field marking, use a proper printed label suited to the location, not a marker scrawl. On a coastal service change, the exterior disconnect's rating plate was sun-bleached blank: the inspector could not verify the rating, and the service had to be re-documented from the manufacturer's records before it passed. Five minutes protecting a plate at rough-in beats that phone call.
sections.florida_note: Exterior Florida labels fade fast. Use UV- and moisture-durable labels outside so required markings survive to the next inspection.

nec2023_change.change: Reconditioned gear has to show who rebuilt it, when, and that it's reconditioned. The original listing mark comes off or is made unreadable, but the nameplate can stay. Required: strip off the original listing mark or deface it so nobody can read it. The rest of the nameplate, ratings included, can stay.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.21 Marking reconditioned equipment

sections.why_it_exists: Markings are the equipment's memory. The ratings tell the next electrician what the gear can take, and hazard marks warn the person about to open it. When a plate fades, or a rebuilt unit still wears its original listing mark, the next worker makes decisions from information that is no longer true.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that any legible mark will do — "DANGER" handwritten in marker on the disconnect. Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it must be a proper, durable marking with recognized signal wording, not handwriting. Second trap: leaving the original listing mark on reconditioned gear so it reads as new. That mark comes off or is voided.
inspection_fails: Field-applied hazard marking handwritten in marker where a proper marking is required.
Rating plate painted over, covered or missing — the equipment cannot be identified or approved.
Reconditioned breaker installed with no reconditioner name or date, and the original listing mark still showing.
Exterior label faded illegible in the Florida sun — the required marking was not durable for its environment.

sections.title: Identification of disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation:
Every disconnecting means has to be legibly marked to show what it shuts off, unless the purpose is already obvious from where it sits and what it feeds.
• The exception is narrow: no separate marking is needed only where the purpose is evident from the disconnect's location and arrangement.
• The marking must be durable for its environment. A pencil scrawl that fades in a Florida garage is not durable.
• On a multi-unit or multi-tenant job, each service disconnect and fault-protection device also has to show where its supply side comes from, so no one opens the wrong gear.
sections.on_the_job: Label every breaker and disconnect with its actual load — 'condenser', 'air handler 2', 'water heater' — not 'spare' labels on live circuits or a directory copied from another house. Update the directory whenever a circuit changes. On a four-plex trim-out in Kissimmee, that means a typed or permanent-marker card at punch, each unit's service disconnect marked with the source that feeds it, and the card re-done the same day any circuit moves — not at the next visit.

In commercial, industrial and multifamily buildings, each disconnect's label has to identify the panel or source feeding it and where that source sits.

sections.why_it_exists: The person opening a disconnect is often in a hurry — a technician chasing a fault, a firefighter killing power, a tenant after a flood. A missing or wrong label means the live circuit stays live while everyone believes it is dead, or the wrong equipment gets killed mid-process. Legible, durable, source-identified marking is what lets a stranger shut the right thing off the first time.

'Spare' labels on live breakers that actually feed loads.

sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'everyone on this crew knows which disconnect is which.' The Code does not accept local knowledge. Unless the purpose is evident from the disconnect's location and arrangement, it gets a legible mark that is durable for its environment. The second trap: a directory that says 'lights / receptacles' on every line is marked — but it identifies nothing.

sections.title: Current transformers
sections.plain_explanation:
This section covers current transformers used with electrical equipment, including how unused current transformers mounted in place are to be treated so their secondary circuits are not left in a hazardous state.
• A CT steps a large primary current down to a small secondary current in exact ratio: a CT marked 400:5 delivers 5 A to the meter while the bus carries 400 A.
• The secondary is not an ordinary circuit. It is built to work into a near-short — the meter burden, or a shorting device at a test block.
• Current-transformer secondaries behave unlike ordinary branch-circuit conductors: an open-circuited secondary under load can produce dangerous voltage, which is why the section and the equipment instructions govern their handling.
• An unused CT that stays mounted gets its secondary shorted and made safe — never left open.
sections.on_the_job: Metered 800 A commercial service in Winter Garden: the CTs sit on the bus ahead of the meter. Swapping the meter, the tech shorts every CT secondary at the shorting block before lifting a single lead, and the spare CT mounted for a future tenant gets its secondary shorted and tagged — not left open. On metered commercial services, never open a CT secondary casually and never leave a mounted spare CT with its secondary open: follow the equipment instructions and this section, or hand it to the person who does this work regularly.

sections.why_it_exists: A current transformer stays tame only while its secondary current has somewhere to go. The primary and secondary ampere-turns balance each other; open the secondary and that balance disappears, the core saturates, and the transformer answers by driving the voltage at the open terminals up until something gives — insulation, an arc, or the person holding the leads. It is a metering device that turns into a voltage hazard the moment its loop is broken.
inspection_fails: Spare CT mounted on the bus with its secondary leads coiled up and left open.
Meter pulled while CT secondary leads were lifted and left dangling, still live from the primary.
Shorting link at the CT test block removed during testing and never replaced.
Secondary leads cut during demolition while the service stayed energized.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the meter is off, so the CT secondary is dead.' Wrong. The primary bus is still carrying load, and the open secondary is exactly when a CT produces its dangerous voltage. A CT secondary is quiet only while it is shorted or connected to its burden — never because the meter stopped reading.
